title: Welcome and Table of Contents
summary: What SS1 Further Mathematics Third Term is about, how to use the notes, and a map of every unit.

p: Third Term has two parts. First is Statistics: finding the typical value of a set of data (measures of location), how spread out the data are (measures of dispersion), and how to compare spread fairly (coefficient of variation). Then comes Operations Research, the 'science of better decisions': linear programming, transportation problems and the assignment problem.

There are many calculations. Set them out in tables, use a calculator carefully, and check by estimating. At the end of each unit are practice questions. They do not count towards a mark; they help you check that you understood. Answer them all correctly to complete the unit.

title: Mean, Median and Mode of Ungrouped Data
summary: The three measures of central tendency for a simple list of numbers, with worked examples and a comparison.

p: Statistics is the branch of mathematics that collects, organises, analyses and interprets data. Measures of location (central tendency) find the centre or typical value where the data cluster. They are the mean, median and mode (and the quartiles, deciles and percentiles in the next unit). Ungrouped data is a simple list of numbers, for example 5, 8, 5, 7, 10.
The mean (arithmetic average) is x̄ = Σx ÷ n, the sum of the values divided by how many there are. Example: 2, 5, 5, 8: x̄ = 20 ÷ 4 = 5.
The mode is the value that occurs most often. Data 2, 5, 5, 8 has mode 5. A data set may have one mode (unimodal), two modes (bimodal) or no mode (no value repeats).

The median is the middle value when the data are arranged in order. Odd number of items: take the middle one. 2, 5, 5, 8, 10 has median 5 (the 3rd value). Even number of items: average the two middle values. 2, 5, 5, 8 has median (5 + 5) ÷ 2 = 5.

Data: 2, 3, 3, 6, 18. Mean = 32 ÷ 5 = 6.4. Median = 3. Mode = 3. The large value 18 pulls the mean up, but not the median. So for data with extreme values, the median is often a better 'typical' value than the mean.
Example 1. For 10, 8, 15, 8, 12: sum = 53, mean = 10.6. Sorted: 8, 8, 10, 12, 15, so median = 10 and mode = 8.
Example 2. Median of 20, 25, 21, 30, 22, 27. Sorted: 20, 21, 22, 25, 27, 30. Middle two: 22 and 25. Median = 23.5.

title: Mean, Median and Mode of Grouped Data
summary: How to find the mean, median and modal value of a frequency distribution using class midpoints, class boundaries and cumulative frequency, with a full worked example.

p: Grouped data are arranged in class intervals with frequencies. We use the class midpoint x to stand for each class.
Mean: x̄ = Σfx ÷ Σf, where f is the frequency, x is the class midpoint and Σf = N.

Median: Median = L₁ + [(N/2 − cfb) ÷ f_m] × C, where L₁ is the lower class boundary of the median class (the class containing the N/2-th item), cfb is the cumulative frequency before that class, f_m is its frequency and C is the class size.

Mode: Mode = L₁ + [Δ₁ ÷ (Δ₁ + Δ₂)] × C, where L₁ is the lower boundary of the modal class (the class with the highest frequency), Δ₁ = f_modal − f_before, Δ₂ = f_modal − f_after and C is the class size.
(b) Median: N/2 = 40, which falls in the class 40–49 (cumulative frequency goes from 21 to 41). L₁ = 39.5, cfb = 21, f_m = 20, C = 10. Median = 39.5 + [(40 − 21)/20] × 10 = 39.5 + 9.5 = 49.0.

title: Quartiles, Deciles and Percentiles
summary: Quantiles that divide data into equal parts, the position formulas, and worked calculations for grouped data.

p: Quantiles divide ordered data into equal parts. Quartiles divide it into 4 parts: Q₁ (25%), Q₂ (50%, the median) and Q₃ (75%). Deciles divide it into 10 parts: D₁ (10%), D₇ (70%). Percentiles divide it into 100 parts: P₄₀ (40%), P₈₀ (80%). Note that Q₂ = D₅ = P₅₀ = the median.
Using the same method as the median: Quantile = L₁ + [(position − cfb) ÷ f] × C, where the position is: Q₁: N/4; Q₂: N/2; Q₃: 3N/4; D₇: 7N/10; P₄₀: 40N/100 = 2N/5.
Use the table from Unit 3 (N = 80).
(a) Q₁: position 20. This is in the class 30–39 (cumulative frequency 11 before, 21 at the end). L₁ = 29.5, cfb = 11, f = 10. Q₁ = 29.5 + [(20 − 11)/10] × 10 = 38.5.

sections.h: Why use the median or quartiles?
p: For skewed data (a long tail on one side), the mean is pulled towards the tail, so the median is often a better typical value. The quartiles show how the middle half of the data is spread.

title: Range and Interquartile Range
summary: Measures of spread: why the centre alone is not enough, the range and its weakness, the interquartile range and the semi-interquartile range.

p: Two sets of data can have the same mean but very different spread. A = 10, 10, 10, 10, 10 and B = 1, 5, 10, 15, 19 both have mean 10, but A has no spread and B has a wide spread. Measures of dispersion tell us how spread out the data are.

Range = highest value − lowest value (ungrouped). For grouped data: Range = upper boundary of the highest class − lower boundary of the lowest class. Weakness: one extreme value (an outlier) distorts it. In 10, 11, 12, 13, 100 the range is 90, though most values are close together.

The IQR measures the spread of the middle 50% of the data. IQR = Q₃ − Q₁. It ignores the lowest and highest quarters, so it is not distorted by outliers. The semi-interquartile range (quartile deviation) is (Q₃ − Q₁) ÷ 2. A larger IQR means the middle half of the data is more spread out.
Example 1. For the 80 marks: Range = 79.5 − 9.5 = 70. Q₁ = 38.5, Q₃ = 57.1, so IQR = 57.1 − 38.5 = 18.6.
Example 2. If Q₁ = 20 and Q₃ = 50, the semi-interquartile range is (50 − 20)/2 = 15.
Example 4. For the 30 puzzle times: range = 24.5 − (−0.5) = 25 minutes; Q₁ = 9.0 and Q₃ = 17.71 (Unit 4), so IQR = 8.71.

title: Mean Deviation, Variance and Standard Deviation
summary: How to measure the average distance of data from the mean (mean deviation) and the root-mean-square distance (standard deviation), with full worked tables.

p: The mean deviation is the average distance of the data from the mean. Ungrouped: M.D. = Σ|x − x̄| ÷ n. Grouped: M.D. = Σf|x − x̄| ÷ Σf. We use absolute values (distances) because otherwise the positive and negative deviations cancel out to zero. A small M.D. means the data are close to the mean.

Variance σ² = Σf(x − x̄)² ÷ Σf. A shorter form is σ² = Σfx² ÷ Σf − (x̄)². The standard deviation is the square root of the variance: σ = √(variance). Squaring gives more weight to large deviations. A small σ means the data are tightly clustered; a large σ means a wide spread. The variance is never negative, because it is a sum of squares.
Interpretation: the average student's mark is about 11.8 marks from the mean, and the standard deviation of 14.75 shows moderate spread.
Why use Σf|x − x̄| and not Σf(x − x̄)? Because the plain deviations add up to zero. What is the relationship between variance and standard deviation? Standard deviation = √variance.

title: Coefficient of Variation
summary: How to compare the consistency of data sets with different means or units using the coefficient of variation, with examples.

p: The standard deviation tells us the spread, but we cannot fairly compare two data sets by their standard deviations if the means are different. Example: Mathematics has mean 80 and SD 2; English has mean 50 and SD 4. Is Mathematics more consistent just because 2 < 4? We need a relative measure of spread. (The CV is a measure of dispersion, not of location, although the source notes list it under 'measures of location'.)

The coefficient of variation (CV) expresses the standard deviation as a percentage of the mean: CV = (σ ÷ x̄) × 100%. It has no units, so it can compare data measured in different units, such as kilograms and metres. A lower CV means more consistent data.
As a rough guide: below about 10%: very consistent; 10% to 30%: moderate; above 30%: high variability and low reliability. A CV of 0% means every value is the same.
Example 1. For the 80 marks, x̄ = 47.25 and σ = 14.75. CV = (14.75 ÷ 47.25) × 100 = 31.22%. The marks are fairly widely spread.
Example 2. Mathematics: CV = (2/80) × 100 = 2.5%. English: CV = (4/50) × 100 = 8%. Mathematics has the lower CV, so it is more consistent.
Example 3. Mean = 20 and variance = 16. σ = 4, CV = (4/20) × 100 = 20%.
Example 4. Engine A has mean speed 200 km/h and SD 10, so CV = 5%. Engine B has mean 80 km/h and SD 6, so CV = 7.5%. Engine A is more reliable even though its SD is larger.
Example 5. Company A: mean salary N50,000, SD N10,000, CV = 20%. Company B: mean N120,000, SD N18,000, CV = 15%. Company B has the more consistent pay.
Example 6. Brand X: mean life 120 h, SD 18 h, CV = 15%. Brand Y: mean 100 h, SD 16 h, CV = 16%. Brand X is slightly more reliable.
Example 7. CV = 20% and mean = 50: σ = 0.20 × 50 = 10.
